questions.question: An angle of 230° is:
solutionSteps: A reflex angle is greater than 180° and less than 360°.
230° satisfies these inequalities.

questions.question: Which condition is not a valid congruence test in general?
solutionSteps: SSS, SAS and ASA determine a triangle up to rigid motion.
Two sides and a non-included angle can describe two different triangles; SSA needs additional conditions.

questions.question: The centre of a non-degenerate parallelogram’s half-turn symmetry is:
solutionSteps: The diagonals bisect each other at O.
A 180° turn about O exchanges both pairs of opposite vertices.

questions.question: If a diameter AB and a point C distinct from A and B lie on a circle, ∠ACB equals:
solutionSteps: AB subtends 180° at the centre.
The angle at C on the remaining circle is half this central angle, namely 90°.

questions.question: Explain how practical measurement led to geometry in India, Egypt and Greece. Distinguish definitions, axioms and postulates, and state Euclid’s five postulates.
questions.finalAnswer: Practical measurement and construction motivated geometry; definitions specify meanings and axioms/postulates are accepted starting rules.
solutionSteps: Land measurement, building and ritual constructions supplied practical geometric problems; Greek deductive geometry organised results into proofs.
Definitions state meanings, for example a circle as points at fixed distance from a centre. Axioms are general accepted principles; postulates concern permitted geometric objects and constructions.
Postulates 1 and 2: draw a straight segment joining any two points; extend a finite straight segment indefinitely.
Postulates 3 and 4: draw a circle with any centre and positive radius; all right angles are equal.
Postulate 5: if a transversal makes same-side interior angles sum to less than two right angles, the two lines meet on that side when extended.

questions.question: Describe a construction of a square on a given segment AB using perpendiculars and equal-length transfer. Relate it to the Sulbasutra practice of constructing squares and justify the result.
questions.finalAnswer: Construct AD and BC perpendicular to AB on the same side, with AD = BC = AB; join C to D.
solutionSteps: Construct perpendicular rays at A and B on the same side of AB.
Transfer length AB onto these rays to mark D and C.
AD and BC are equal and parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram. A right angle makes it a rectangle.

Adjacent sides AB and AD are equal, hence it is a square. This illustrates the square-construction problem found in the Sulbasutra tradition; it is not a claim that this is the sole historical procedure.

questions.question: Define a ray and an angle. State the linear-pair theorem and its converse. Prove vertically opposite angles are equal when two lines intersect.
questions.finalAnswer: A ray has a starting point and extends in one direction; an angle is formed by two rays with a common endpoint. Vertically opposite angles are equal.
solutionSteps: A linear pair consists of adjacent angles whose non-common arms are opposite rays; their sum is a straight angle, 180° = two right angles.
Conversely, if two adjacent angles sum to 180°, their non-common arms form a straight line.
For intersecting lines, let consecutive angles be α, β, γ. Linear pairs give α + β = 180° and β + γ = 180°.
Subtract equal β from the equal sums to obtain α = γ. Repeat for the other pair.

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 65°. Find its corresponding angle, alternate interior angle, and adjacent same-side interior angle. State the converse tests for parallelism and transitivity of parallelism.
solutionSteps: Corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal for parallel lines, so both are 65°.
Same-side interior angles are supplementary: 180° − 65° = 115°.
Conversely, equality of corresponding or alternate interior angles, or supplementary same-side interior angles, implies parallelism.
Distinct lines parallel to the same line in a plane are parallel to each other. Parallel lines are coplanar and do not meet.

questions.question: Explain why a triangular frame is rigid while a four-sided frame can change shape if its joints rotate. For AB = AC in triangle ABC, prove the base angles equal, stating matching vertices.
questions.finalAnswer: A triangle’s three side lengths fix its shape; ∠ABC = ∠BCA.
solutionSteps: Three side lengths determine a triangle by SSS, whereas four side lengths alone do not fix a quadrilateral’s angles. Diagonal braces split a frame into rigid triangles.
Compare triangles ABC and ACB: AB = AC, AC = AB and BC = CB.
SSS gives congruence with A ↔ A, B ↔ C and C ↔ B.
Corresponding base angles at B and C are equal. This is why triangular bracing is useful in structures.

questions.question: State SAS, SSS, ASA, AAS and RHS precisely. Explain why RHS does not justify using SSA for every triangle.
questions.finalAnswer: RHS applies specifically to right triangles with equal hypotenuse and one corresponding leg.
solutionSteps: SAS: two corresponding sides and the included angle; SSS: three corresponding sides.
ASA: two corresponding angles and the included side. AAS: two corresponding angles and any corresponding non-included side; the third angles are equal.
RHS: two right triangles have equal hypotenuses and one corresponding leg. The other leg follows from Pythagoras, reducing the problem to SSS.
General SSA lacks a right-angle/hypotenuse condition and may be ambiguous. The correspondence and included-angle requirement must be checked.

questions.question: Give a precise definition of a quadrilateral using four distinct coplanar points, no three collinear, and their successive sides. Prove that a simple quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides equal is a parallelogram.
questions.finalAnswer: The union of AB, BC, CD, DA is a quadrilateral; opposite sides equal imply a parallelogram.
solutionSteps: Join A to B to C to D to A, with four distinct coplanar vertices and no three collinear. A simple quadrilateral has no crossings other than adjacent sides meeting at vertices.
In simple ABCD draw AC. Given AB = CD and BC = DA, AC is common.
Triangles ABC and CDA are congruent by SSS.
Matching alternate interior angles imply AB ∥ CD and BC ∥ AD, giving a parallelogram.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, P and Q are midpoints of AB and AC. Prove PQ ∥ BC and PQ = BC/2 by extending PQ to S with QS = PQ.
questions.finalAnswer: PQ is parallel to BC and half its length.
solutionSteps: Extend PQ through Q to S with QS = QP. Since AQ = QC and vertical angles at Q are equal, triangles AQP and CQS are congruent by SAS.
Hence AP = CS and AP ∥ CS. With AP = PB, the segment PB is equal and parallel to CS.
PBCS is a parallelogram, so PS ∥ BC and PS = BC.
P, Q, S are collinear and PS = 2PQ. Therefore PQ ∥ BC and PQ = BC/2.

questions.question: A circle has radius 5 cm and a chord AB of length 8 cm. Find the perpendicular distance of AB from the centre O and prove why the perpendicular bisects the chord.
questions.finalAnswer: Distance 3 cm; the perpendicular bisects AB.
solutionSteps: Let M be the perpendicular foot. Right triangles OMA and OMB have equal hypotenuses OA = OB and common leg OM.
RHS gives AM = MB, so each half of the chord is 4 cm.
OM² = OA² − AM² = 25 − 16 = 9; OM = 3 cm.
Conversely, if M is the midpoint, SSS makes the adjacent angles at M equal and supplementary, hence each is 90°.

questions.question: Describe how to construct the unique circle through three non-collinear points. State where its circumcentre lies for acute, right and obtuse triangles.
questions.finalAnswer: Intersect two perpendicular bisectors; the circumcentre is inside, at the hypotenuse midpoint, or outside respectively.
solutionSteps: Construct perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC. Non-collinearity ensures they meet at a unique O.
O is equidistant from A and B, and from B and C, so OA = OB = OC.
Draw the circle of radius OA. Any centre of a circle through all three points must lie on both bisectors, proving uniqueness.
For an acute triangle O is inside; for a right triangle it is the hypotenuse midpoint; for an obtuse triangle it is outside.
